questions.stem: A 50 year old man attends the emergency department with burning central chest pain that started an hour after a large curry. He has had similar episodes for 2 months, worse when he lies down at night, with an acid taste in his mouth. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. ECG is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heartburn after meals, worse lying down, with acid regurgitation is GORD once cardiac pain has been excluded (normal ECG and troponin); angina is exertional.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down, with acid regurgitation and a normal ECG and troponin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

elim: Sharp pain eased by sitting forward with widespread ST elevation.
RUQ pain radiating to the shoulder, not burning retrosternal pain with acid taste.
Intermittent chest pain with dysphagia, not related to lying flat after meals.
Brought on by exertion and relieved by rest, not by meals and lying down.

steps.x: **D. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.** Burning chest pain after meals, worse lying flat + acid taste = GORD.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with a BMI of 35 who smokes 20 cigarettes a day has 3 months of sour fluid coming up into his mouth, especially when he bends over to tie his shoelaces or lies down after his evening meal. He has burning behind his sternum most evenings. He has no weight loss or dysphagia.

questions.e: Obesity and smoking predispose to GORD, which causes heartburn and acid regurgitation, worse lying down or bending; achalasia gives undigested food and dysphagia.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: sour fluid coming up into his mouth
lies down after his evening meal
steps.x: Obesity and smoking are reflux risk factors; acid regurgitation on bending or lying is classic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

elim: Progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food.
Food bolus obstruction in young atopic men.
Epigastric discomfort without acid regurgitation.
Epigastric pain related to meals, not regurgitation on bending.

steps.x: **D. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.** Acid regurgitation on bending/lying in an obese smoker = GORD.

questions.stem: A 46 year old secondary school teacher has 4 months of a hoarse voice that is worst in the morning, frequent throat clearing and a dry night-time cough. She does not smoke. questions.e: GORD can present atypically with chronic cough and hoarseness from acid reaching the larynx overnight; a normal laryngoscopy excludes a mass.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Morning hoarseness, night cough and posterior laryngeal redness: acid reaching the larynx overnight.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

Causes a weak, breathy voice with a paralysed cord, not redness.
No rhinitis or postnasal drip, and laryngeal redness with heartburn points to acid.
Visible nodules from voice overuse, not posterior laryngeal redness.

steps.x: **A. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.** Hoarse in the morning + night cough + heartburn = GORD.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has had heartburn most days for 15 years and has bought antacids over the counter rather than seeing a doctor. He is obese and smokes. questions.q: Which is the most likely complication he is at risk of?
questions.e: Chronic GORD causes Barrett's oesophagus (columnar metaplasia of the squamous lining), which can progress to oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Long-standing acid exposure changes the squamous lining to columnar.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Barrett's oesophagus.

An infection causing painful swallowing in the immunosuppressed, not a long-term lining change.
Caused by portal hypertension.
Oesophageal web with iron deficiency anaemia.

steps.x: **A. Barrett's oesophagus.** Long-term GORD -> Barrett's oesophagus.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with Barrett's oesophagus under surveillance has 2 months of progressive dysphagia to solids and 6 kg weight loss. OGD shows an irregular, ulcerated stricture in the distal third of the oesophagus arising within the Barrett's segment. Biopsies are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological type of tumour?
questions.e: Barrett's oesophagus is a precursor to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, typically in the distal third; squamous cell carcinoma arises higher, from squamous mucosa.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Barrett's columnar metaplasia is the precursor of distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Adenocarcinoma.

elim: A submucosal spindle-cell tumour, not arising from Barrett's mucosa.
A benign smooth muscle tumour.
Mainly a lung tumour.
Mostly upper and middle oesophagus, linked to smoking and alcohol.

steps.x: **A. Adenocarcinoma.** Barrett's -> distal adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has 6 months of daily heartburn and acid regurgitation that persist despite omeprazole for 8 weeks. She has no red flags. Her GP refers her for an upper GI endoscopy, and she stops omeprazole 2 weeks beforehand.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding at endoscopy?
o: Dilated oesophagus with a tight lower sphincter
Erosions of the distal oesophageal mucosa
Tortuous dilated veins in the distal oesophagus
questions.e: Acid refluxing into the oesophagus causes irritation and, with repeated exposure, oesophagitis with distal mucosal erosions; rings suggest eosinophilic oesophagitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Repeated acid exposure injures the distal oesophagus first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Erosions of the distal oesophageal mucosa.

elim: Describes achalasia.
Describes eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Oesophageal varices from portal hypertension.
Suggests carcinoma; she has no red flags.

steps.x: **B. Erosions of the distal oesophageal mucosa.** GORD at endoscopy = distal reflux oesophagitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has 6 weeks of burning behind his breastbone on nights out, after takeaways late at night and after several pints of beer. It eases with an over-the-counter antacid. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting or weight loss. Abdominal examination is normal. His temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heartburn after late meals and alcohol, relieved by antacids, without red flags is GORD; it is managed first with lifestyle changes such as avoiding late meals.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Heartburn triggered by late meals and alcohol and eased by antacid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

elim: Dysphagia to solids and liquids, not heartburn eased by antacid.
Dysphagia and food impaction, often with atopy.
Epigastric pain or fullness without heartburn.
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with vomiting.

steps.x: **D. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.** Heartburn triggered by late meals and alcohol = GORD.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with 20 years of poorly treated reflux has 1 year of slowly progressive difficulty swallowing solids, with food sticking low in his chest. His heartburn has actually improved. His weight is stable. Barium swallow shows a short, smooth, tapered narrowing of the distal oesophagus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his dysphagia?
questions.e: Chronic acid injury heals with fibrosis to form a benign (peptic) stricture: slow solid dysphagia, stable weight, smooth tapering; cancer has an irregular narrowing and weight loss.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Slow, progressive solid dysphagia with stable weight and a smooth tapered narrowing after long-standing reflux.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Benign oesophageal stricture.

elim: Gives a dilated oesophagus with a bird's beak and dysphagia to liquids too.
Usually rapid progression, weight loss and an irregular shouldered narrowing.
Causes high dysphagia, gurgling and regurgitation of old food.
A thin ring causing intermittent bolus obstruction, not progressive dysphagia.

steps.x: **B. Benign oesophageal stricture.** Long GORD + slow dysphagia + smooth narrowing = benign stricture.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant with her first baby has heartburn most evenings and acid coming up into her throat at night. She had no reflux before pregnancy. Her blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg and urinalysis is normal. There is no epigastric tenderness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
o: Progesterone relaxing the lower oesophageal sphincter
questions.e: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, including the lower oesophageal sphincter, reducing oesophageal tone, which is why pregnancy is a risk factor for GORD; normal BP argues against HELLP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
New reflux in pregnancy with normal BP: hormonal LOS relaxation (plus uterine pressure).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Progesterone relaxing the lower oesophageal sphincter.

elim: Causes vomiting, jaundice and liver failure.
Epigastric pain with hypertension, haemolysis and low platelets.
Severe vomiting in the first trimester.
Less likely; reflux symptoms in late pregnancy are typical of GORD.

steps.x: **E. Progesterone relaxing the lower oesophageal sphincter.** Reflux in pregnancy = progesterone relaxing the LOS.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with a BMI of 33 has years of heartburn and regurgitation that are much worse when she lies flat. Upper GI endoscopy shows mild distal oesophagitis, and the gastro-oesophageal junction lies 4 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch. She takes no regular medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her reflux?
questions.e: A hiatus hernia disrupts the normal anatomical anti-reflux barrier at the gastro-oesophageal junction, a major cause of GORD alongside a defective LOS and obesity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: much worse when she lies flat
gastro-oesophageal junction lies 4 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch
steps.x: The GOJ has moved above the diaphragm: a sliding hiatus hernia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hiatus hernia.

elim: She takes no regular medicines.
Not relevant at 59.
No Raynaud's or skin tightening, and the endoscopy shows a hernia.
Gastrin excess with multiple ulcers.

steps.x: **A. Hiatus hernia.** GOJ above the diaphragm = hiatus hernia causing GORD.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is referred by his dentist, who has noticed erosion of the enamel on the inner surfaces of his back teeth. He describes waking with a sour, bitter taste in his mouth and a burning feeling in his chest after big dinners. He has no vomiting or binge eating. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acid regurgitation in GORD can reach the mouth overnight, giving a sour taste on waking and dental erosion, with heartburn after meals.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: waking with a sour, bitter taste
burning feeling in his chest after big dinners
steps.x: Acid reaching the mouth overnight erodes enamel; heartburn after meals.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

steps.x: **C. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.** Sour taste on waking + heartburn + enamel erosion = GORD.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has 5 weeks of burning retrosternal discomfort after meals and acid regurgitation, worse lying down. She has no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, bleeding or anaemia. Examination is normal. She asks which test will prove she has reflux.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to the diagnosis?
questions.e: GORD is a clinical diagnosis in most cases; endoscopy is reserved for red flags, age 55 or over, or failure of treatment.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Typical symptoms, young, no red flags: no test is needed to diagnose it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical diagnosis from the history.

elim: Reserved for atypical or refractory cases before surgery.
Not needed for typical symptoms.
For motility disorders or before fundoplication.
There are no red flags and she is under 55.

steps.x: **C. Clinical diagnosis from the history.** Typical GORD without red flags = clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had heartburn and regurgitation for 4 months. He has taken omeprazole 20 mg daily for 8 weeks with good adherence and lifestyle changes, but his symptoms persist. He has no weight loss, dysphagia or bleeding. His haemoglobin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Endoscopy is the gold standard if GORD needs confirming and is indicated for symptoms persisting over 4 weeks despite medical management, or age 55 or over.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Symptoms persisting over 4 weeks despite treatment need direct confirmation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper GI endoscopy.

Does not show mucosal disease.
For colorectal cancer, not reflux.
For suspected Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy.** Failed treatment = upper GI endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has reflux treated with omeprazole for a year. For 3 weeks she has passed black, tarry stools and feels tired. She has no dysphagia. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Increase omeprazole and review in 8 weeks
questions.e: Red flags in reflux (weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding, anaemia, recurrent dyspepsia) warrant urgent endoscopy; melaena indicates an upper GI source.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
GI bleeding and anaemia are red flags in dyspepsia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent upper GI endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has had intermittent heartburn for 2 months. He has no weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding or anaemia, and his examination is normal. He is not sure which foods set it off and wants to sort it out without tablets if he can. His urea breath test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Without red flags, a meal diary to identify triggers is a simple lifestyle intervention in GORD, alongside the H. pylori breath test; invasive tests are not needed.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.

clues: no weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding or anaemia

steps.x: **C. Meal and symptom diary.** No red flags + unknown triggers = meal diary.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has dyspepsia and heartburn. She has been taking omeprazole 20 mg daily that she bought from a pharmacy for 3 weeks. She has no red flags. Her GP wants to test her for Helicobacter pylori with a carbon-13 urea breath test.

Take a double dose of omeprazole

PPIs suppress H. pylori and give false negatives.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop omeprazole 2 weeks before the test.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with a BMI of 31 has heartburn most nights about an hour after going to bed. He eats his main meal at 10 pm, just before bed. He has no red flags. He would like advice before trying medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate lifestyle advice?
o: Eat earlier, lose weight and raise the head of the bed
Take a large meal at bedtime
questions.e: First-line lifestyle measures for GORD are weight loss, avoiding late meals and elevating the head of the bed.

steps.x: Late meals, obesity and lying flat all promote reflux; correct each.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Eat earlier, lose weight and raise the head of the bed.

elim: Gives brief relief but stimulates acid secretion.
Lying flat worsens reflux.
Fat delays gastric emptying and relaxes the LOS.

steps.x: **B. Eat earlier, lose weight and raise the head of the bed.** GORD lifestyle: lose weight, eat earlier, raise the bed head.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has had heartburn and regurgitation for 3 months. She has lost weight, stopped eating late and raised her bed head for 6 weeks with little improvement. She has no red flags and her urea breath test is negative. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: After testing, a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole is first-line drug treatment for GORD alongside lifestyle changes.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Lifestyle has failed and there are no red flags: start acid suppression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Omeprazole for 4 to 8 weeks.

elim: H2 antagonists are added later if symptoms persist on a PPI.
Rare option for refractory disease.
Her breath test is negative.
No red flags and under 55.

steps.x: **C. Omeprazole for 4 to 8 weeks.** GORD drug treatment: PPI (omeprazole) first.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with endoscopically confirmed mild reflux oesophagitis takes omeprazole 20 mg once daily. After 6 weeks, taking it correctly before breakfast, his heartburn is only partly improved. He has made the lifestyle changes advised. His repeat assessment shows no red flags.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: With an inadequate PPI response, increase the dose or try a different PPI such as lansoprazole; surgery is a rare option for refractory disease.

Partial response with good adherence: optimise the PPI first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Increase the omeprazole dose.

elim: A prokinetic not recommended for routine GORD.
Reserved for refractory cases after medical options fail.
He still has symptoms needing treatment.
Weaker than a PPI.

steps.x: **B. Increase the omeprazole dose.** Partial PPI response: increase dose or switch PPI.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with GORD takes high-dose lansoprazole twice daily. Her daytime symptoms are controlled, but she still wakes most nights with heartburn. She sleeps with the bed head raised and eats her evening meal early. Endoscopy last year showed mild oesophagitis only.
questions.q: Which drug class is most appropriate to add?
questions.e: If symptoms persist on a PPI, an H2 receptor antagonist such as famotidine is added; calcium channel blockers, nitrates and antimuscarinics worsen reflux.

Nocturnal breakthrough acid on a PPI: add a night-time H2 blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: H2 receptor antagonist.

Relaxes the LOS and worsens reflux.
Relaxes the LOS and worsens reflux.
Does not treat reflux.

steps.x: **C. H2 receptor antagonist.** Night symptoms despite PPI = add an H2 antagonist (famotidine).

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has had severe reflux for 5 years. He gets diarrhoea and headaches with every PPI he has tried and has stopped them. Lifestyle changes have not helped. Endoscopy shows oesophagitis, 24-hour pH monitoring confirms acid reflux, and manometry shows normal oesophageal motility.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Fundoplication is a rare surgical option for GORD refractory to (or intolerant of) medical treatment, after reflux is confirmed and motility checked.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Proven reflux, refractory to and intolerant of medical treatment, with normal motility.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Laparoscopic fundoplication.

elim: For malignant obstruction.
For achalasia.
For gastric cancer or complicated ulcers.
For achalasia.

steps.x: **C. Laparoscopic fundoplication.** Refractory, proven GORD = fundoplication.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has had reflux for years, controlled with omeprazole. For 6 weeks food has been sticking in his chest, first with bread and meat and now with soft food. He has lost 4 kg. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Double the omeprazole dose and review in 8 weeks
Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy
Request a barium swallow and see in routine clinic
Test for H. pylori and treat if positive
questions.e: Red flags such as dysphagia and weight loss need urgent endoscopy via the 2-week wait referral pathway (NICE); doubling the PPI delays diagnosis.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.

clues: food has been sticking in his chest
steps.x: Progressive dysphagia and weight loss in long-standing reflux: suspected cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy.

Routine imaging delays a cancer diagnosis.
Does not address new dysphagia.
For dyspepsia without red flags.

steps.x: **B. Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy.** GORD + dysphagia = 2-week wait OGD.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has heartburn and regurgitation of acid after meals. Oesophageal manometry shows a low resting pressure at the gastro-oesophageal junction with normal peristalsis in the oesophageal body. A student asks what causes his symptoms.

o: Failure of the LOS to relax on swallowing
Incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter allowing retrograde flow
Increased gastric acid production by a gastrinoma
questions.e: GORD results from an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter, which allows retrograde flow of acidic gastric contents into the oesophagus.

steps.x: A weak LOS lets gastric contents flow back.

Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, not a low LOS pressure.
Describes diffuse oesophageal spasm.
Causes oropharyngeal dysphagia.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with GORD starts omeprazole, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. Two weeks later her heartburn has gone. A pharmacology student asks which cells the drug acts on and how long its effect on each pump lasts.

Irreversible inhibition of the proton pump in parietal cells
Neutralisation of acid in the gastric lumen

Stimulation of mucus secretion by surface cells
questions.e: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) on gastric parietal cells, so acid secretion recovers only as new pumps are made; famotidine blocks H2 receptors.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
PPIs bind the H+/K+ ATPase of the parietal cell irreversibly.

steps.x: Irreversible inhibition of the proton pump in parietal cells.

That is how antacids work.
Not the PPI mechanism.
Describes misoprostol or sucralfate effects.

steps.x: **B. Irreversible inhibition of the proton pump in parietal cells.** PPI = irreversible H+/K+ ATPase inhibition in parietal cells.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with erosive reflux oesophagitis on endoscopy is treated with high-dose omeprazole for 8 weeks. Repeat endoscopy shows that the distal erosions have healed. A student asks why the drug allowed the oesophageal lining to recover.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the healing?
o: Killing of H. pylori in the oesophagus
Less acid in the refluxate allowing mucosal repair
questions.e: Repeated acid exposure causes oesophagitis; PPIs reduce acid secretion, so the refluxate is less acidic and the mucosa can heal, even though reflux itself continues.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Repeated acid exposure caused the oesophagitis; removing the acid lets it heal.

steps.x: Less acid in the refluxate allowing mucosal repair.

H. pylori does not colonise the oesophagus.

PPIs have no direct effect on squamous cells.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with systemic sclerosis has Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin over her fingers and 6 months of severe heartburn and regurgitation. questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her reflux?
o: Reduced oesophageal motility with a weak LOS
questions.e: GORD is caused by a defective lower oesophageal sphincter, reduced oesophageal motility (poor acid clearance) or a hiatus hernia; systemic sclerosis causes both of the first two.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Smooth muscle fibrosis weakens both peristalsis and the LOS.

steps.x: Reduced oesophageal motility with a weak LOS.

Not linked to systemic sclerosis.
She is not overweight.
An upper oesophageal pulsion diverticulum.

steps.x: **E. Reduced oesophageal motility with a weak LOS.** Systemic sclerosis reflux = weak LOS + poor motility.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had GORD for 20 years. Surveillance endoscopy shows salmon-coloured mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsies show intestinal-type columnar cells with goblet cells and low-grade dysplasia. He asks what this may lead to.
questions.q: Which is the most likely sequence leading to cancer in his oesophagus?
o: Squamous hyperplasia, squamous dysplasia, squamous cell carcinoma
questions.e: Repeated acid exposure causes oesophagitis; over time the squamous epithelium undergoes columnar metaplasia (Barrett's oesophagus), a precursor to adenocarcinoma through dysplasia.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Acid injury, then columnar metaplasia (Barrett's), dysplasia, then adenocarcinoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oesophagitis, columnar metaplasia, dysplasia, adenocarcinoma.

Strictures are fibrotic, not premalignant.
Linked to smoking and alcohol, not Barrett's.
Varices are unrelated to cancer.

steps.x: **B. Oesophagitis, columnar metaplasia, dysplasia, adenocarcinoma.** GORD -> oesophagitis -> Barrett's -> dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has 6 weeks of new heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals. She has never had reflux before. She has no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or bleeding, and her full blood count is normal. She drinks coffee daily. Her GP decides she should have an upper GI endoscopy.
